B.explanation: This is the fractional strain $\Delta l / l \approx 5.1 \times 10^{-4}$, not yet multiplied by 100 to convert to percentage contraction.

hints: Notice the wire was stretched by a tension of $20 \text{ N}$ before snapping, so the fractional contraction equals the tensile strain $\Delta l / l$ under that load.
Connect stress to the $5.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$ diameter using $stress = F/A$ with $A = \pi (d/2)^2$, then use $E = stress/strain$ with $E = 2.0 \times 10^{11} \text{Pa}$.
Calculate strain as a decimal first, then multiply by 100 for percentage, and check whether you halved the diameter to get the radius.
walkthrough: Find the cross-sectional area from the diameter. Radius $r = d/2 = 2.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}$, so $A = \pi r^2 = \pi (2.5 \times 10^{-4})^2 \approx 1.96 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^2$.
Find the tensile stress that was in the wire. $stress = F/A = 20 / (1.96 \times 10^{-7}) \approx 1.02 \times 10^8 \text{Pa}$.

Use the Young modulus to find the strain, which equals the fractional change in length. $E = stress/strain$, so $strain = stress/E \approx (1.02 \times 10^8)/(2.0 \times 10^{11}) \approx 5.1 \times 10^{-4}$.
Convert the fractional contraction to a percentage. $percentage = strain \times 100 \approx 5.1 \times 10^{-4} \times 100 = 5.1 \times 10^{-2}$ %.
